name: Seven and one
text: Up at Knappers' Deep, on the lip of Hound Down, the knapper woman keeps a lamp lit at the shaft head every night for the night shift. The roof came down on them eleven winters back. She says they knock. Seven and one, the overman's count. My cousin heard it, lying in the turf with his ear to the old shafts.
variants: Don't lie down on the old shafts round Knappers' Deep. You'll hear them knocking, and once you've heard it you hear it everywhere.

name: Cheap floorstone
text: The man at the Flint Pits is selling floorstone at six marks the sack, and he never dug a sack of it. The Larkbourne Boys go down the ladder at Knappers' Deep and dig it from under Nell Knapper's feet. She won't go to the Wardens. Says the Wardens capped her father in.
variants: If you want black flint cheap, ask at the Flint Pits and don't ask where from. Knappers' Deep, it is. The Boys.

name: Standing on the lip
text: Rookdown won't go up past the mill after dark this summer. The Hum Stone on the lip hums with the Toll now, and the dead come up the cliff out of the Hush to stand by it and listen. They don't do anything. Merrowby's bellwright is camped out there with a cart of hand-bells. He doesn't do anything either.
variants: The old stone on the Brow's lip has started humming. The grey's come up round it on the cliff side. Don't stand there after dark.

name: The cracked bells
text: Two of Merrowby's family bells have cracked since the spring, the Cresswells' and the Ashdowns', in the night, hanging in their trees with nobody near them. Godwin the bellwright says it's the diggers cutting the bronze off the Hum Stone. Godwin also says the Toll is trying to tell us something, so.
variants: You heard about the Cresswells' bell? Cracked in the night. Then the Ashdowns'. Godwin's gone out to the Brow about it.

name: The stone that walks
text: You know Wake Barrow, the one with the oaks on, up on Hound Down? The Crowle woman's lamp goes out every night now, and the big stone in the front's coming out of its hole a hand at a time, like something's leaning on it. Pilgrims coming down the road say there's folk stood behind the barrow after dark. Nobody's been buried up there since the Ash Winter.
variants: The stone's out at Wake Barrow. Far enough to get by, Tamsin Crowle says, and she won't go by it.

name: The barrow-wives' oaks
text: There's seven oaks on Wake Barrow, one for every barrow-wife that sat the wakes up there. My gran said you could tell how the Vale's dead were lying by the oaks. The one at the front's dropping its leaves in July. That's Ebba Crowle's.
variants: Ebba Crowle's oak on Wake Barrow is dying. Leaves down in July.

name: Blossom at midnight
text: You know the old press on Wassail Knap, past Hazelcombe? Dead orchard, forty years. It came into blossom one night this spring, every tree, at midnight, and in the morning there was fresh toast in the old Wassail Tree. Three of the Hazelcombe pickers went up to pick what it bore. They're not back. Pip Applegarth's sat up there in a hut ever since.
variants: There's singing comes up out of the cellar grates on Wassail Knap. The old songs. My nan knew the words and she won't say them.

name: Forty-one
text: Old Strawe up at the Scarecrow Moot set forty. Everybody knows it's forty, he chalks it on his post. This summer there's forty-one, and he can't say which farm the new one came from, and he knows every farm on the down.
variants: The rooks sit on every scarecrow on the Moot but one. Strawe says that's how you can tell.

name: Letters from Harewell
text: Wenna at the Letter-Cote still writes to the four quiet villages every week, Mullbourne and the rest, the ones off the Roll Stone. Always has. The doves always come back empty. Only now they don't. Now some of them come back with answers, in a child's hand.
variants: Send a dove from the Letter-Cote if you've lost your way. It comes back with the road in its eye, Wenna says.

name: The candle that goes out
text: Up at the Candle-Wheel the Dippers keep a candle lit for every name on the Wardens' Roll, and not one has ever gone out. Tallis Dipper says one goes out every night now, the same one, and in the morning the name under it's been scraped off the shelf. She lights it again. She doesn't know whose it was.
variants: Give Tallis Dipper a coin and a name and she'll dip it a candle and keep it lit. My gran had one dipped for her own name, just in case.
